speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance arising out of his announcement of his intention to introduce legislation to impose curbs or restrictions on the granting of consumer credit. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY AND NORTH AMERICAN SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources a question suggested by statements attributed to United States officials following the President's statement earlier in the week. Has the government of the United States, or spokesmen on its behalf, indicated directly to the government of Canada that in the view of the United States government our Canadian oil policy constitutes a threat to the security of North America?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY AND NORTH AMERICAN SECURITY
speechtext:
In our conversations earlier in the year the question of security did come up. I believe the term "security" as

it is used with respect to oil supply means security of supply. I do not think the reference is to national security in terms of defence. Certainly United States policy over the years has been based on the concept of security of supply from domestic sources. We have maintained-and I think this is so-that the Canadian position is different, that our policy cannot be identical to theirs because of the different circumstances that prevail in Canada.

maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY AND NORTH AMERICAN SECURITY
speechtext: A supplementary question. Has anybody on behalf of the United States government suggested to the government of Canada that we ought to reduce our imports of oil into Canada in order to foster a secure supply of oil in North America?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY AND NORTH AMERICAN SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, different views have been stated from time to time by different officials in the course of discussions. There are, of course, two views on the question of our importation of oil. One is directed toward security of supply, which might be diminished in the event that offshore oil, by reason of circumstances prevailing in other countries, could not be obtained. The other view concerns making our markets available to Venezuelan oil, as does the United States. I think this is in accord with the view taken by the United States as well as ourselves in regard to our foreign policy toward Latin America.

maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY AND NORTH AMERICAN SECURITY
speechtext: One further supplementary question. Would the minister specifically answer the question whether the United States has made representations to Canada to the effect that we ought to reduce our imports, and thus our reliance upon imports, of oil from outside the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY AND NORTH AMERICAN SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think that representation has ever been made. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out that our discussions with the United States since last March, when the President and the Prime Minister originally took the initiative in the matter of energy discussions, have been sporadic and on a broad plane. No firm positions have been taken by the United States or by Canada; and no position such as suggested by the hon. gentleman has been taken.

maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY AND NORTH AMERICAN SECURITY
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Will the minister undertake to make a full statement on motions next week outlining the state of the negotiations between Canada and the United States on energy policy?

speechtext:
The bill is designed to redraft two sections of the present act to put them into language that will mean what they were thought to mean when they were enacted by Parliament and what they were thought to mean by the administration administering the Act. They involve no change in principle in any way and no matter of substance. They are purely technical. In one of them, the change becomes necessary by reason of an interpretation put on one of the clauses by a court, and the other amendment was made necessary as a result of a question that was raised-and this matter did not go to court- as to what the existing language meant. The matter was dealt with in the committee; it is purely technical and no change in substance is involved.

subtopic: PAROLE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext:
I think the minister put it very fairly when he said that these are, in fact, technical changes designed to overcome some of the problems that were encountered when the former measures were interpreted. Indeed, so technical was the language of the bill, and so difficult the study thereof, that even the best minds in the House of Commons frequently found themselves in great difficulty. I refer of course to the members of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. However, we did our best with it and passed it after a good study. Sometimes bills are passed unanimously in committee, sometimes they are passed on division. This one, we felt, was passed in confusion. None the less, as the minister noted, it makes two important technical corrections to what we thought was the intention in the existing legislation. But I think it should be added that these changes have not taken away any rights for which people have fought and which they obtained in the courts. These changes conversely, will be of benefit to the people who are now undergoing penitentiary sentences. In other words, we are not depriving anybody of


Parole Act
a specific right. We are clarifying the technical language, to preserve the rights that we thought they enjoyed already.
It might be of interest to note that there is a retroactive provision in the bill, since the section shall be deemed to have come into force on the 26th day of August of last year. The reason for it is that was the date of the proclamation of the parole sections of the omnibus Criminal Code with which we dealt during an earlier session of this Parliament. Part of the difficulties for which this bill is the remedy arose because of some imprecise drafting which did not fit the intentions of the administration and, to be fair, of all members of the House, in relation to the very important matter of parole.
Perhaps I could be allowed to make two very quick points in concluding my brief remarks. The first is that the study of this bill gives us all an opportunity to pay respect to one of the great public servants of Canada. I refer to Mr. George Street, the chairman of the National Parole Board. I am very pleased that Mr. Street's tenure of office has been extended by this government. He was appointed by the administration headed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). He is truly an outstanding Canadian, and perhaps part of the ease with which we finally stumbled out of the technical jungle in which we found ourselves was because we knew that Mr. Street was prepared to light a torch and lead the way for us. We on this side of the House, and I am sure on the other side as well, have great faith in that gentleman.
The other point I would like to make very briefly deals with the fact that when we have technical bills such as this, which really are measures designed to bring about what we originally intended to bring about, the procedure should be short and simple. I can think, for example, of my own bill relating to some sections of the divorce act with which difficulties have been experienced in the court. I hope we can devise a law reform procedure whereby such bills as this one, and the one I am sponsoring, can get rather quick study without opening up the subjects they deal with the widespread discussions that go on and on for days and days. In other words when we need technical remedies we have to find a way of achieving them rather quickly, otherwise minor and technical reforms in the law have to wait for an unjustified period of time. Fortunately, this criticism does not apply to this case and I say on behalf of my colleagues that we support the measure.

Mr. Speaker, I recently pointed out the importance of considering without delay the way in which to change our system of weights and measures. The scientific or mathematical demonstration of the importance of the metric system is so conclusive by itself that it is not necessary to take it up again.
The process to be followed effects obviously the very subject matter of the bill on standardization. We wish this change would be carried out as soon as possible with as few drawbacks as possible so that Canada may have the same system as most countries in the world. Of course, our decision is closely tied to that of our neighbours to the South, the United States. Nevertheless, we could already bring about this change in a number of fields without adversely affecting our industrial and commercial relations with the United States.
Mr. Speaker, we therefore wholly agree with the principle that it is necessary to establish standards systems.
In closing I would like to repeat that it would perhaps be advisable to consider the possibility of coming to an understanding with an association existing already, and see if it would not be possible for the government, particularly in this austerity period, to effect savings by accepting a kind of mixed association with a view to protecting the interests of all Canadians.

speechtext:
I hope the remarks coming from the opposition side of the House indicate my remarks are hitting the point. May I continue, after having been so rudely interrupted?
As I said, consumer standards, apart from food and drug standards have, in my view, suffered neglect in Canada, and this is a serious deficiency. There is an increasing pres-

Standards Council oj Canada sure to fill this gap from informed consumers, from the Consumers Association of Canada and from the Consumers Council which I appointed. Some progress has been made in limited fields such as garment sizing and care labelling of textiles, but there is an enormous job still remaining to be done. Despite the very considerable accomplishments of the Canadian Standards Association, the Canadian Government Specifications Board and a number of other standards-making bodies -all of them have been doing exceedingly good work-there is an urgent need for a truly representative and truly national body to promote and co-ordinate development by standard-setting agencies which will benefit the ordinary people, the ordinary consumers of this country.
I believe that the proposed standards council of Canada will have an essential role in achieving this aim. It will represent the whole spectrum of agencies concerned with and interested in standards in Canada. It is quite natural that such a body as the standards council of Canada should have heavy representation from industry because of the highly technical nature of many of the issues in the field of standards. However, I can forecast confidentally that consumers will have, and must have, an important voice in the work of the council. There will clearly be participation by my department, by the Consumers Association of Canada and by the ten provinces which will have a real interest in promoting the consumer interest.
It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that the standards council of Canada will give priority attention to the problem of product safety. There is ample evidence that an unwarranted number of Canadians are being killed and maimed every year in accidents involving seemingly innocent household products. Products that are inadequately designed, insufficiently labelled or easily subject to misuse cause both untold suffering and great economic loss. This morning I announced new regulations under the Hazardous Products Act which would deal with the labelling of a wide range of consumer chemical products. In 1967, the last year for which figures are available for this country, there were over 15,000 cases of children under four years of age being poisoned from household products. We announced this morning appropriate regulations governing the labelling of these products so that, hopefully, we can develop voluntarily some proper lids for these products and cut down on these kinds of poisonings.


Standards Council of Canada
The economic cost to this country as a result of such injuries and poisonings in terms of providing hospital and medical services and in terms of losses suffered by those who are employed is enormous. Anything we can do to develop greater product safety and eliminate accidents arising from faulty products will be of great economic benefit to Canada, altogether apart from any humanitarian considerations with regard to personal suffering and injury. We need to improve our statistics on household accidents, but enough clear evidence exists to show conclusively that more rigorous safety standards for consumer goods would contribute greatly to the public good. In the United States, the National Commission on Product Safety has been examining over 2,000 commonly used consumer products. Its report to be published later this year will bring to light, I am quite sure, inadequacies of design and of performance in many products sold widely in the United States and Canada and will highlight the need for better consumer product standards and regulations. I hope that the Standards Council, working with the private agencies, can promote and develop great numbers of voluntary standards that will govern products and product safety.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS AND POWERS, ORGANIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The Hazardous Products Act passed by this House last session provides the framework for the most comprehensive consumer product safety programs in the world, and provides the legislative tool which can be used to back up some of our safety standards. Once satisfactory standards have been developed by the council in co-ordination with private standards-setting agencies, there will be no excuse for allowing dangerous or substandard consumer products on the market. In some special areas, it is possible for the federal government to develop product safety standards, but in most other areas it is essential to rely on the special knowledge and technical competence of industry, safety organizations and the medical profession; and the council will provide an excellent vehicle to bring together this knowledge, this expertise and this competence. It is hard to overestimate the need for an agency such as the standards council to sponsor a consistent and broad gauged plan which will lead to the elimination of many of the booby traps in Canadian homes. Consumers will look to the council to exercise leadership and to co-ordinate the development of voluntary standards in this area.
I want to dwell briefly on another responsibility of the proposed standards council of Canada, its role in relation to converting to the metric system. There has been, so far as I can judge, widespread support expressed for the very excellent and forward looking statement that was issued by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce on the question of metrication just before Christmas. This statement makes it clear that the metric die is cast, even though the timing of conversion is indefinite and a great many very complex problems remain to be resolved. A great deal of attention has been paid to the implications of converting to the metric system for industry and commerce, but I would also like to note that any general adoption of the metric system in Canada has profound implications and advantages for consumers.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
The cornerstone of a market system is that the consumer has full, complete and factual


information so that he can properly judge the product he is buying and make an intelligent comparison of it with other like products. The metric system would greatly enhance the consumer interest in proper information, product and package comparability. The existence of a standards agency, with balanced representation from all sectors of the economy, will be vital if we are to deal satisfactorily with the abandonment of our traditional measures of pounds, quarts, inches and gallons and the adoption of a far more logical and consistent system of weights and measures. The conversion process, as the experience of Britain makes clear, is not a simple one, and I believe that the standards council of Canada will have a major contribution to make in easing problems of conversion which inevitably must be made. Hopefully, this can be achieved in the future with a minimum amount of difficulty and problems. We are creating an agency which, I think, can ease our way to conversion.
Finally, I want to say a word about international standardization. While it is obvious that the development of standards is of crucial importance to international trade in industrial machinery, building materials and so forth, there is increasing concern being shown over international standards for consumer goods. The International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission have recently established a joint body to deal with consumer standards. The ISO has an active technical committee on consumer questions. Recently, the OECD established a committee on consumer policy. In addition, a number of ad hoc international committees have been convened to deal with special problems. Many of these committees are dealing with issues which are important to Canadian industry and to the Canadian consuming public. I feel that it is important that Canada's participation in these international standards associations be as strong as possible and that we assure that all international developments are kept under careful scrutiny. From the point of view of prestige and continuity, I believe that it is absolutely necessary for Canada to be represented by an agency created by the Parliament of Canada, which will reflect all the interests involved in any discussions or negotiations on the international standards scene.
There has been some hesitation about this bill, Mr. Speaker. Noting the advantage to Canadian consumers of greatly improved systems of voluntary standardization, I find it

Standards Council of Canada very difficult to understand why that hesitation exists. I can only conclude that such hesitation stems from a misunderstanding of the intent and purpose of the standards council which will have great benefit, not only to Canadian industry, commerce and trade, but also to the ordinary Canadian consumer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has gone to considerable length to put on the record the allegation that the official opposition is not concerned with standards in Canada or with protecting the consumer. I say to the minister if his external brilliance is any indication of his comprehension of the facts, it is an absolute misrepresentation. What we say is the Canadian Standards Association is already set up. This association is doing a good job and we do not believe it is necessary for the government to be sticking its nose into every part of society today. We have the new Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs as well as several other agencies, including the Food and Drug Directorate. These departments would only have to give assistance to the voluntary agency which is already established. We could proceed from there with standards in other areas.
In my opinion, Bill C-163 is just another duplication. It is an unnecessary government exercise. Many attempts have been made by this government to introduce through the back door what can be termed as seemingly innocuous legislation, but this bill is certainly a strong candidate for first prize. The government is asking us to accept the need for a federal corporation to foster and promote the voluntary standardization of weights and measures, quality and performance of goods, and industrial and commercial methods and practices.
The Canadian Standards Association has been functioning for 50 years. It has a very good reputation. There have been few complaints registered against this association. The CSA operates independently of industry, government and supplier to establish standards for consumer items manufactured and sold in Canada. It works with other standards groups throughout the world to establish and maintain standards for consumer goods in the markets of international commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
Will the hon. member accept a question? If it is true that the CSA is so perfect, why do some of the officials of that organization keep referring to the major


Standards Council of Canada changes that are taking place in the organization and to the tremendous new programs that they have in mind for the future?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS AND POWERS, ORGANIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think there is anything wrong with referring to programs for the future. The government talks about the future all the time. It should not criticize a voluntary association that looks to the future in the same way. I cannot see any legitimacy in that argument.
Throughout the 50 years of its existence, the CSA has built up a reputation for excellence that places Canada high in the opinion of other countries. The best testimony of this is the fact that many countries accept Canada's standards as their own. The CSA trade mark is accepted without question by countries with which Canada trades in consumer goods.
Even in the face of this evidence, Mr. Speaker, I would not suggest that the present CSA methods of operation should not be examined. It is possible that an independent study of the entire CSA operation should be undertaken to determine whether the CSA is, in fact, adequate to present needs. It may well be that the CSA is not competent in some areas to manage the changeover to the new international system of units known as the metric system.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
All these probabilities I will concede. If the reorganization of existing standards were proposed I would not hesitate to support such a move. But I cannot assent to the complete reorganization of the present arrangements or to the assumption that once a government agency is created a much better job will be done. Look at the operation of other government undertakings, the Post Office, for example. I learned the other day that 140 years ago mail sent by the California Express from Missouri to the west coast arrived in eight days. The other day a man told me it had taken ten days for a letter sent from Ottawa to reach Vancouver. How can the minister expect us to have much faith in the type of reorganization he is proposing? Consider the operations of the Wheat Board. It turns out, we learned yesterday, that the board was paying four cents a ton commission on the shipment of Canadian grain in certain circumstances, and someone pointed out that a salesman can make almost as much selling a dozen cases of dog-food as he can by shipping large quantities of Canadian wheat. How can any faith be placed in any new organization which the govem-
ment may set up when this is the kind of performance we have learned to expect from those which already exist?
The government is proposing to set up a new federal body to operate alongside the CSA. There is no indication whatever that it will receive the co-operation from all concerned which is now available on a voluntary basis. The preamble to the present bill states that a government agency to be known as the standards council of Canada will foster and promote the voluntary acceptance of standards in Canada and also serve as the Canadian representative at meetings of standards groups of foreign countries. All this, the CSA has been doing for 15 years. In paragraph 4 (b) of clause 2 the bill gives the Council power to accredit other organizations which are concerned about the establishment of standards. This is the thin end of the wedge, the first indication that Bill C-163 is not as innocuous as the minister pretends it is. Paragraph (g) of the same clause gives the minister's council the power to establish its own trademark as the new Canadian standards trade mark. Already the government is saying that the old Canadian standards mark is not good enough-that the new council will have its own mark. Yet the minister went to great lengths yesterday to tell us that everything would be done voluntarily.
Further, the bill authorizes the new agency to accept and spend moneys appropriated by Parliament, to acquire and hold real property, to alienate that property at pleasure, and to do such other things as are incidental or conducive to the attainment of the objects and exercise of the powers of the council. The bill also prescribes the number of people who shall be members of the board. The council is to consist of an executive council made up of a president and some 57 members. Clause 14 gives the council authority to appoint such other officers and employees as may be necessary for the proper conduct of its work. In other words, this is yet another case of an empire being built.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS AND POWERS, ORGANIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
We have already seen what has happened in the case of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I am not arguing that some of these things ought not to be done, but there seems to be no end to the new empires which are being built with the approval of this government. I maintain that when we read this bill the picture we get is not that of a harmless body of conscientious


citizens looking over the shoulders of the Canadian Standards Association. This proposal has all the earmarks of a complete takeover, and the instruments to accomplish it are well spelled out in this legislation.
The minister was at great pains to explain that this could all be done through co-operation. Yet the bill spells out all that is necessary for a complete take-over and the eradication of the facilities which now exist. If this is the intention of the government-and having studied this measure I cannot believe that any hon. member could take a different view-why does the minister not tell us in clear terms that the administration is getting into the standards business and that everyone else is getting out? However he may have tried to disguise the intention, it is clear to anyone who has taken the trouble to read this document clause by clause. We are confronted,. here, not only with machinery for a takeover, but with an example of duplicity.
Aside from the fact that the services which the Canadian Standards Association have been providing for so long will, from now on, be hampered by bureaucracy, there is the question of cost, something which should always be considered. The only reason put forward by the government for contemplating the establishment of a standards council in the first place was that the CSA had asked for funds from the government to defray part of its costs.
The fact is, the CSA has been self-supporting since its inception. I know the minister can answer by saying that the charges have in fact been paid by industry and passed on. But nothing will convince me that less money will be needed, or that these services can be provided at lower cost to the public if the government takes over the standards council. The request to which I referred a few moments ago was a request for a grant to cover membership dues in the international organization for standardization, of which the Canadian association is a member. The fee amounts to $50,000 a year, I believe compared with the CSA operating budget of some $4,500,000 a year.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Another reason advanced by the government, after the fact, is that other western nations have government-operated standards organizations. If we examine other examples of government-operated standards agencies, the only one similar to the one proposed is in South Africa. France has been put forward
Standards Council of Canada as an example, but I believe in their case the government only elected one of their members to the board, the president; the actual work of the board was carried on within a voluntary structure, as is the case with the CSA. Britain, Germany and Sweden have organizations similar to what the minister would establish here, and are something akin to the present functions of the CSA.
This is a time when the government is telling the Canadian people to follow its example and spend wisely. I suggest that the measure before us today does not comply with that theory. It is not calculated to accomplish any goal except that of adding to the load of the taxpayers, with questionable benefits to consumers. I suggest the government could work through our present organizations with some direction from the department.
I have found a clause on the last page of the bill, almost the last clause. I suggest it should really have been one of the first clauses and that the bill should have been built around it. Clause 18 provides:
The Council shall be deemed to be a charitable organization in Canada as described in paragraph (e) of subsection 35(1) of section 62 of the Income Tax Act-
That is a rather exciting observation to find buried in the bill. This council is going to be called a charitable organization-one other charity, I suppose, that is to be supported by the taxpayers of Canada. It is also of interest to note that the bill has still to pass the House, and I would think there were sufficient members in the House of good judgment not to hasten its passage unduly. The government has already appropriated money for the council in the estimates. Probably it thought that the bill might slide through before the estimates were published, I do not ktjow. I think we should all consider the bill most carefully. I and a lot of my colleagues share the view that we should not be duplicating a service that can be better performed by an existing organization, one that is self-sustaining.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess I am the man for whom the bell tolls. Anyway, I am delighted with the opportunity of saying a few words this afternoon on Bill C-163 to establish a standards council of Canada. I am delighted also to see the genial minister in his seat, smiling as usual through storm and stress. I have a first question which I think might be indicative of what I am going to say later. My question is, why voluntary standards? We propose voluntary standards in this particular field, yet we do not have voluntary standards when we judge criminal behaviour. However, of the things that have gone on as a result of our lack of standards in this country verge on that kind of behaviour.
The slogan, "let the buyer beware", in my view is a sordid phrase, I think it is much more appropriate to an age much earlier than our own and out of place in this complex society. Perhaps it was reasonable in a more simple society in which the products were simple. You went to someone you knew to make your purchases and there was craftsmanship rather than factoryship at work. Certainly, in the earlier days there were not the vast number of synthetic products in terms of plastics, synthetic textiles and that sort of thing. The various chemical additives have by their very nature, placed these products in a position where the average member of the public is unable to make a decision based on his own particular knowledge or the feel of a particular piece of cloth. He has no idea really what he is buying, nor does he know very much about the sizing of it, its shrinking, lasting qualities or methods of cleaning.
I think it is self-evident that we need standards. I believe, too, that the consumers not only in this country but in the United States as well have been rooked for years because of the phrase, let the buyer beware. I think this is an aspect of our society that has had tacit approval for far too long. It is time for the government to take a much more active role to see that reasonable standards, not only of safety as the Minister of Consum-

er and Corporate Affairs mentioned this morning but also of quality, be available in a readily accessible and meaningful form to the people who are the purchasers of our country.
I think perhaps the fact that the Consumer Reports, a United States magazine, has such a wide sale in Canada is an indication of distrust of the standards we now have; the kind of packaging and labelling standards for North America products. I do not believe that particular magazine, which is supported by subscribers, would enjoy such wide support from the general public if people felt confident that they could depend upon the quality or the labelling of the products they purchased.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
This organization which publishes Consumer Reports, as I mentioned earlier, is an independent organization not financed by manufacturers or by consumers, except in the sense that they buy the magazine. It consults and conducts tests, and I have used its information many times while contemplating the purchase of some item that was going to be fairly costly. I think perhaps many members of this House realize that this particular group not only tests various products but also rates them and puts them in a rank order so that people have an opportunity to make an intelligent decision on their purchases rather than depending upon the often spurious advertising for them. I think the standards council of Canada might consider, after it develops somewhat its activities, the same type of practices as those engaged in by the Consumer Report magazine and the group that sponsors it. We need to set up independent testing laboratories and not be influenced by the conflict of interest of the various manufacturers. They are more interested in pushing their products than they are in ensuring that the products are always of like quality or always safe.
The other thing the Council might do, and this is where the word "voluntary" comes under question, is to rate these various products. If there are, for example, 15 manufacturers of electric ranges-there are probably only three-the Council should do independent testing and rate them so that people will know they are getting value for their money, or at least will be able to buy what they desire with information available to them. So, those two points, testing and rating, should be considered by the new council. What happens when you do not have this? What happens is what has been happening, not only in manu-

facturing industries but also in service industries that is that people who do not have the expertise are constantly being defrauded. The well known case is the one of the automobile service garages in Montreal. This business has come in for a great deal of criticism by a group of people who know the field and make their investigations of repair charges available to the general public.
So the question, then, is not really about the need for standards but whether this bill will really accomplish the provision of standards useful to the Canadian public. I note that under section 116, subsection 33D of the Criminal Code amendments of last year, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has broad powers to control advertising. He mentioned just before lunch, the matter of protecting the consumer, but he has broad powers now under this section which reads as follows:
Everyone who publishes or causes to be published an advertisement containing a statement that purports to be a statement of fact but that is untrue, deceptive or misleading or is intentionally so worded or arranged that it is deceptive or misleading, is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years, if the advertisement is published.
I do not know whether or not there have been any charges laid under this section, but I wonder if it would apply to any of the campaign literature of the Liberal party. This might be an interesting question. But people demand standards on which they can depend, there is no doubt about it.
Last weekend, which I spent in my constituency, I was visited by a number of people including an old gentleman who came to see me about the problem of standards. He was complaining about, of all things, dress sizes for older women. Presumably he was considering purchasing one for his wife, but he did not tell me that.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has given us during this debate a clear and concise technical report. Later on the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) told us how the Canadian people would like to see these standards established.
If I may, I should like to go back a little in order to give the background of the subject, which will be useful since some members have said that we were trying to establish standards in a brand new field and that therefore, we did not know where we were going.
In order to do that, at the international and domestic level, we have to go back to the year 1700 B.C. At that time, the king of Babylon had been immortalized as a statue holding in his hand a measure 10i inches long. Therefore, we are not really breaking ground in this field and all researchers agree that it is the oldest existing specimen of a linear measure.
Therefore, measuring would have existed long before writing. The Roman people, in compliance with the wishes of Alexander the Great, established and used a measuring system which spread all over Europe. However, it is only at the beginning of the industrial revolution, namely at the start of this 21774-39i
DEBATES	5007
Standards Council of Canada century, that countries started to establish national standards in co-operation with manufacturers.
Essentially, standards are a means available to the consumer to indicate precisely his needs to the manufacturer, which requires of course the co-operation of several and various interested groups.
In that field, Great Britain established a national agency in 1901; Canada, Germany and the Netherlands in 1917; the United States in 1918 and Sweden, in 1920. Since then, several other countries also established standards councils.
There are now 55 countries with different agencies at the national level, almost all of them belonging to international organizations, namely the I.S.O. and the Electro-Technical Commission (IEC). In most of those countries, those agencies are totally or partially subsidized by the government.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we must establish at the international level, standards acceptable not only to member countries, but also other countries that have no national commissions or agencies but nevertheless take part in international trade.
Since the last war, the countries using the standards established by both above-mentioned associations have doubled. Therefore we should not be surprised at the spectacular increase in regulations these last few years.
The IEC was created in St. Louis, in the United States, in 1904 and now has its headquarters in Geneva. Canada has been a member of that organization since 1908.
The ISO was established in 1946 in London. Canada has been a member since then. It has succeeded the National Standards Federation, established in 1926, that had to discontinue its activities on account of the 1939-45 war.
Technical committees, especially from the ISO, combine national standards and establish international standards concerning a great variety of products such as paper, copper, pipes, boilers, agricultural machinery, etc. On account of Canada's importance in the export field, Canadian standards in the technical field are accepted with great respect in foreign countries.
The participation to ISO and to IEC is of great benefit. Therefore, our country must be ready to participate still more actively in the technological development of developing countries.
In Canada, standardization has developed considerably at the industrial and governmen-


Standards Council of Canada tal levels because, as I said before, we are on exporting and we understand the need for international standards.
There are two parallel agencies in Canada. In fact, the Canadian Standards Association deals with the private sector. I would like to emphasize this point. Moreover, as I said before, there is a government agency which deals with the public sector and with industry. These two structures operate in the same manner thanks to committees that were created according to needs and where government and industry are represented.
However, it is difficult to eliminate the duplication of research and consequently the task becomes very difficult. Once it is established, the Standards Council of Canada will become responsible since it will represent Canada within the ISO and the IEC for the preparation of international and national standards.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has received, I think, many publications concerning the establishment of standards for the sizing of garments. Indeed, the government was asked to establish in this field a Canadian standard and to give other instructions concerning consumer products. Therefore, this question becomes an urgent priority.
The control of standards in the private sector has been in force since 1917 as was mentioned. In the public sector, it has been in existence since 1934.
Therefore, it was decided to establish the Standards Council of Canada after studying the situation that prevailed in the United States, in Great Britain and in France as we have closed links with these countries.
In the United States, the ASTM, The American Society for Testing Materials, and the SAE, the Society of Automotive Engineers, control about 65 per cent of American standards.
There are, however, in that country several hundred other associations that are active in various sectors. That is the source of many problems at the present time. They would appear to be interested in watching closely the debate on the bill now before the House, Bill C-163.
Mr. Simpson, assistant secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, in February 1970, and I quote:
[Mr. Trudel.1

The lack of a strong (US) standards institute is the reason European officials have thus far refused to allow this country to Join an agreement certifying that electronic components can be traded across national boundaries.

This is one of the reasons why they follow our activities very closely.
Various countries have been mentioned. In this regard, I should like to point out that in England, the B.S.I., that is the British Standards Institution, a national organization, is responsible for standardization. The English government finances that project in a proportion of 50 per cent.
The department responsible for this in England is the Department of Technology. The adoption of the metric system, which has been discussed by two or three members, will depend on the decision of the Standards Council of Canada.
In France, the Association frangaise de normalisation-AFNOR-through committees, controls most standards, with already number in excess of 5,000.
In his remarks, the member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) wondered why we should not do as other major countries and leave to a private organization the responsibility for standards.
I should like to refer again to the few countries I have mentioned, particularly Great Britain.

Like the proposed standards council of Canada, BSI is an independent body government by an executive board on which government departments are officially represented; is incorporated under royal charter, which authorizes it to establish its own by-laws; receives substantial financial assistance from the British government-about 50 per cent of its income-

It represents Great Britain in international voluntary standardization activities; administers the national certification mark, BSI's "Kite" mark, and is responsible for directing the technical aspects of Great Britain's conversion to the metric system.
Another country that I would like to look at, Mr. Speaker, where you will find such similarities is France, to which I have previously referred. Like the proposed standards


council of Canada, AFNOR is an independent non-profit organization in Which producers, users and government are represented. It coordinates the work of standardization bureaus, of which there are 34, represents France in international voluntary standardization activities; administers the national certification mark; and submits an annual report, including financial statements to the French government.
In the United States, and I have referred to the United States before, like the proposed standards council of Canada, ANSI is an independent non-profit federation of technical, professional and trade organizations. It acts as a national co-ordinating institution for voluntary standardization in the United States; serves as a national clearing house for information of United States and foreign standards; does not engage in the preparation of standards; does not operate testing or inspection laboratories; represents the United States in international voluntary standardization activities, for example, ISO and IEC, and approves national or USA standards.

Despite the anxiety felt by the member for Gander-Twillingate and the member for Battle River (Mr. Downey), I believe that the situation in those three big countries is similar to the one described by the minister and that there would not be any conflict of interests.
In England, France, Japan and even Sweden, the controlling structures are therefore much more closely related to government. Those countries do not experience the duality in private and public sectors as it exists in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore wholly support the creation of the Standards Council of Canada, which will be responsible for co-ordinating the policy of Canadian standards and ensuring the participation of Canada to the establishment of international standards.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill relating to a field that is quite narrow but exceedingly complex, I think, for the average Canadian and even for us members, I must say we are being asked to give our consent to changes in the long standing methods by which Canada has instituted standards in various fields that are so necessary to modern living. To name only a few products for which standards are necessary, there are building products such as

Standards Council of Canada cement, tiles, gypsum products, washers and threads, oil and gas furnaces, transformers, the automobile, safety ferrous metals, nonferrous metals, timber products, wood preservation, welding, etc. Indeed, there are a whole host of materials that are used in daily work for which standards are necessary.
Up until now, this work has been carried on by the Canadian Standards Association which is a non-profit, non-governmental association to provide a national standardization body for Canada. This organization receives requests for standardization, investigates their desirability and arranges for the formation of committees with both the makers and users, scientific and technical societies, inspection authorities and government departments, to determine standards that will be acceptable to all concerned. These must meet with the approval of many provincial bodies who state what standards shall be used.
The Canadian Standards Association has provided leadership to benefit the consumer and also the manufacturer. In general, CSA seems to have been very successful in doing its part in promoting good, reasonable standards for Canada. CSA has at the present time over 650 standards committees with over 4,000 representatives of consumer technical organizations, federal and provincial governments and industry. Now, as well as these services, the CSA provides certification or approval services through its laboratories and agents in Canada and abroad. All in all, the CSA seems to have made itself a most useful means of effecting Canadian standardization that has been adequate for our needs.
Now, what is the government proposing in bill C-163 which will provide for the establishment of a standards council of Canada. Although the minister in his introduction of the bill continuously referred to the furtherance of voluntary standardization, the bill seems to go much further than would appear necessary to effect this. Either the government has decided at this time to move in on the Canadian Standards Association and assume their duties or it has deliberately made the powers of the bill so broad that it will at some time in the future be able to assume all the voluntary functions of the Canadian Standards Association without the necessity of bothering to ask Parliament for the necessary authority.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Perhaps this would be a good time to look at countries faced with similar problems. In
5010	COMMONS
Standards Council of Canada the United States, which has an economy much more complex than our own, there was introduced into the House of Representatives a bill for a "co-ordinating and clearing house agency" which dealt with the subject of standardization. The bill was not proceeded with and the United States counterpart of CSA, known as the American National Standards Institute, or ANSI, was devised to deal with problems of standardization. It seems particularly significant that CSA was used as a model for the United States body. Now, the minister is introducing legislation which in effect says that the existing CSA is not adequate or cannot be improved and that, therefore, we must have a government controlling body over the whole of the voluntary standards field.
In a report last year which confirmed that ANSI, which was modelled after the CSA, was working reasonably well, the president of ANSI stated that five years previously there had been a need for a more effective organization to use improved procedures for the voluntary co-ordination and promulgation of standards that would be recognized as United States standards, both nationally and in international standardization activities. Five years later ANSI is reasonably satisfied with its progress. Continuing his report, the president of ANSI said:
Of at least equal importance to the primary findings was the Panel's conclusion that 'the development of standards should be left to the several private organizations already active in the field.' It also stated that: 'the voluntary nature of the development, promulgation, and use of 'USA Standards' is emphasized by the Panel in rejecting any suggestions of compulsion that would be in conflict with the principles of free enterprise.
By and large these recommendations have been accepted and implemented through recognition that the technical competence required for the development of standards resides in the 160 technical societies, trade associations, labor and consumer organizations confederated in the American National Standards Institute.
The president of ANSI further stated:
These facts also illustrate rather dramatically the problem that government agencies would face in recruiting the numbers, variety, and levels of specialized competence required to staff necessary standardization activities of the United States, if prime responsibility for this work should ever become a function of government. The extent and nature of cooperation between the government and private sector is the correct topic of debate. The question is not where the source of authority should reside-in government or the private sector-but rather how best can competence be organized and made most effective.
The minister raised a number of points illustrating the need for this legislation. He

mentioned the need for representation for all concerned, meaning that some sectors of the community may not be adequately represented. I would be the first to admit that, especially in such an immense, widely varied and technical field, it might be difficult to find people conversant with all aspects of a problem. But I doubt if the government will be able to do better than the CSA has done. This organization, through its procedure for establishing committees of producers, consumers, government authorities and scientific and technical people, has ensured that a reasonably broad representation of interest is assembled in its standards-writing and review comments. The CSA is also planning to establish a consumer advisory council to the CSA's board of directors. There does not seem to be all that need for the setting up of a separate group to provide these services; indeed, it would seem that if the government did this it would end up with the same people.

In the international field,
Canadian industry participates in ISA work and CSA is at present very active in ISD projects. I will, therefore, follow with interest what the minister will propose in committee.
The Canada standards council we are told will make us aware of international trade strategy. Well, government does not always seem to have all the answers in this field. The grading of western grain is under the rigid control of the Board of Grain Commissioners, and for the first time in 20 years this matter is to be revised extensively. For many years wheat should have been considered and sold on a protein basis. It is generally considered we are five years or so behind our competitors in the grading of our wheat. Similar long standing deficiencies occur in connection with other grains. There have been repeated calls by all segments of agriculture and business, ranging from farm organizations to grain companies, for changes in grading regulations. Where were the alert watchdogs of the government who should have signalled long ago that changes were needed in our grain standards. They must have been asleep.
These are only a few of the matters that the minister and his officials will be required to answer in committee. The minister has protested at length that his interest is wholly in voluntary control and the furtherance of standardization. Indeed, the minister doth in many ways protest too much, making him suspect. It was stated in a briefing by the Director of the Office of Science and Technology, that, "It is not proposed that the Council engage directly in standards formulation, testing or certification activities which will continue to be carried out by existing standards organizations". Yet the powers of the council, under the provisions of sub-

(c)	establish and circulate criteria and procedures relating to the voluntary preparation, approval, acceptance and designation of standards in Canada in those fields;

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always listen with interest to the arguments advanced by the opposition. I am


Standards Council of Canada sympathetic to many of them. Yesterday I listened with particular interest to my good friend, the hon. member for Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Lundrigan). He comes from a good province. Yesterday, he demonstrated beyond all possible doubt that there is no herring shortage in that province-at least red herring! I have never seen in this House more tattered regiments of arguments paraded than were presented yesterday afternoon. What it amounts to is that we are going to be dragged, kicking and struggling, into any kind of reform in this field which has been crying for reform for many years.
The hon. member spoke of the tried and true. He said there is something about experience and longevity which should be respected, indeed enshrined. Sin is old and sickness is old. No one would advance the criterion of age alone in order to advance arguments in favour of these evils. What we must do, without being partisan about it, is place this proposal under the microscope of this House and attempt to make some dispassionate judgments. Some of the arguments advanced by the hon. members for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie), Battle River (Mr. Downey) and Gander-Twil-lingate are representative of a tunnel vision.
At the outset, I want to deal this afternoon with some of the international aspects of the measure before us. I also want to touch on some of the concern expressed by members of the opposition. Many of us appreciate the assurances given by the minister when he ably presented this measure yesterday afternoon. Members are aware that at least some members of the Canadian Standards Association, and I use the designation "some members" advisedly, are fearful of the measure we have before us. This is a long respected and established body. I would be unfair if I did not acknowledge the tremendous value which the CSA has been to the lumber industry in the province of British Columbia. This association has done a grand job. It has enabled the lumber products of my province to become competitive in the markets of North America and the markets of the world. What we really want to see in Canada is the same kind of excellence demonstrated by the CSA in, for example, the area of lumber, extended throughout British Columbia, the other provinces in Canada and, indeed, the entire Dominion in as many industrial and economic fields as possible.
It has been suggested if the bill is enacted that a federal government corporation will be given the power to supersede the Canadian

Standards Association as the national agency for voluntary standardization in Canada. I do not believe that. Hopefully, this bill will reach the committee stage. I do not think hon. members will support this spurious proposal for a six months hoist advanced by the fearful member from Newfoundland. When the bill is before the committee, further assurances can be obtained from the minister and examined in greater detail.
I want to see the CSA carry on its useful and beneficial activities in this and other areas. The assurances given by the minister indicate that some of the fears which have been expressed are unfounded. The Council is designed to foster, promote and co-ordinate voluntary standardization activities in Canada. It is not intended that the Council should engage in standards formulation, and this has to be emphasized because the point has not even registered with the opposition, testing or certification activities, which would continue to be carried out by standards organizations such as the CSA. I, for one, want to see the CSA carry on its good activities inspired and assisted by government. Nor will the council duplicate other activities of such organizations. This is brought out very clearly in several sections of the bill. For example, Clause 4(1) reads:
The objects of the Council are to foster and promote in Canada the voluntary standardization-
Section 4(2) states that the Council, in carrying out its objects, may:
(a)	promote co-operation among organizations concerned with voluntary standardization in Canada in those fields to co-ordinate standardization activities and develop common standards and codes;
(b)	promote co-operation between organizations concerned with voluntary standardization in Canada in those fields and departments and agencies of government;
Yet it is suggested there is something sinister about this provision. The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate said, "I smell a rat". I suggest he was smelling a red herring in his own back yard.
In addition, reference is made to organizations engaged in standards formulation, testing and certification and to the Council's relationships with such organizations in several other paragraphs of section 4(2), namely paragraphs (d), (e), (f), (i) and (j). I am not going to go into all the details. Members have this bill in front of them. From this it is quite clear that the council is not intended to supersede and replace existing standards organizations, but rather to assist such organ-
March 13, 1970	COMMONS
izations to play a larger and more effective role in formulating and promoting the use of standards in Canada.
The CSA can play an integral and expanding role in standards formulation in this country. I speak with enthusiasm about the contributions this organization has made. Some people say this council will be controlled by the civil service. It is intended that the council should provide a national focus for voluntary standardization embracing all Canadian interests. Members of the council will be drawn from all regions of the country and all sectors of the economy. It would not be appropriate to limit the groups from which membership would be drawn as, for example, has been done in the case of the Science Council of Canada Act, which sets up a specialized organization.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Section 12(1) of the bill provides for an executive committee consisting of the president, the vice-president and seven other members, of whom six shall be selected by the council and one shall be designated by the Governor-in-Council. The standards council will be responsible for selecting six of the nine members of the executive committee. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the CSA will be invited to join and be given a role in this executive. I am sure the majority of hon. members in this House would support such an idea. This is not an attempt to end the existence of the CSA.
The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate put forward the other day the radical reform proposal of the Conservative Party. The most imaginative proposal he had to make was that we should hoist this bill for six months which would, of course, constitute its death sentence. Beyond that, they want to maintain the status quo. It was suggested there should be more time for discussion. Mr. Speaker, there have been four years of discussion with no limit imposed on the nature of the representation made by the organizations involved, including the CSA. No item was declared non-negotiable. The question might well be asked: What could be done in six months which was not accomplished in four years? The legislation is the product of consultation and detailed discussion. If it is imperfect, let it go to the committee as soon as possible, where improvements may be made. The proposal of the official opposition as enunciated by three of its representatives is an arid, sterile, and unproductive answer to a longterm need.

speechtext:
I hope the hon. member will extend to me the same courtesy as I extended to him the other day, and hear me out. Some officers of the CSA say the CSA is doing the job now. This assertion was advanced as a valid argument by the hon. member who has just walked out of the chamber. The bill, he told us, was an example of needless duplication. Yet despite the fact that it was granted letters patent in 1914, the CSA has not taken any real interest in at least 35 major areas during the 50 years of its operation. I will read some of them from the list I have here: petroleum products, aircraft materials and components, automotive vehicles and products, chemicals, hospital equipment, shipbuilding, mining equipment, building codes and practices, electronics, nuclear energy and agricultural food products. For one reason or another, perhaps for lack of resources, the CSA has not moved into these areas.
The standards council will be established to encourage the CSA to do so, and to take action in these and other areas. It will make use of existing organizations which are concerned with standardization. There is no intention that the council would, or should duplicate the functions of others.

Here are Members of Parliament, supposedly speaking with the interest of their provinces at heart, fighting to maintain a situation which does not give them any kind of representation at all upon a board whose decisions affect them. They may say otherwise, but I believe western Canada and the Maritimes deserve better representation on the standards-making body than they are getting on the present CSA board.
While the CSA has done excellent work in some areas, the board of directors has lacked balanced representation. Surely, it should be representative of all groups having a major interest in standards, including consumer, producer, trade and government groups; it should be impartial, with no group predominating; it should possess the confidence of the public at large; it should have a wide scope of activity and be concerned with all sectors in all parts of the country, and it should be aware of the country's international strategy.
What is this international strategy? We are in the midst of a tough trade war. We know that Canada lives by trade. In a world which is decreasing, as it were, in size, not only in the sphere of communication but also in the sphere of economics, there must be the strongest possible Canadian government representation within the international standards organizations. Two organizations are responsible for most international standards, apart from those which regulate food and drugs and which are usually covered by domestic legislation. They are the Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission.
The IEC is the older of the two bodies, having been established in St. Louis, U.S.A., in 1904. Its headquarters are now located in Geneva. It has carried out most useful work throughout the years since then, but only in the field of electrical standards. Canada has been a participating member country for many years. The ISO was established in 1946, but it then represented a reconstruction of a body first established in 1926 and known as the International Federation of National Standardizing Associations which disappeared during the strife of the Second World War. Canada was represented at the founding meeting in London, England of ISO. The field of activity of ISO covers all technical standards, with the exception of those handled by IEC.

These examples illustrate how ISO work affects major Canadian export industries. First, in the fall of 1955 it was discovered, almost by accident, that a draft ISO recommendation for unalloyed aluminum ingots was to be considered at a meeting scheduled to be held in Paris little more than one week later. This particular draft contained a detailed provision for major and trace elements that, by failing to recognize some important characteristics, would have effectively obscured the high quality available in Canadian aluminum and reduced its competitive position; and as we all know, aluminum is one of Canada's most important exports.
Arrangements were quickly made for two senior technical representatives to attend the meeting in France as fully accredited Canadian representatives. The Canadian viewpoint was presented, the draft was amended and the resulting recommendation is now in use throughout the world with no detriment to Canadian aluminum.
Second, at a meeting in 1961 the ISO committee on hewn, sawn and planed timber developed draft recommendations using metric units only, despite the fact that 58 per cent of the world's timber is sawn to inch dimensions. Fortunately, Canada joined the ISO committee in 1962 and was represented at the 1963 meeting held in Moscow. Thanks to the excellent spirit of informed compromise prevailing at the meeting, and the cooperation of the chairman, both systems of measurement are now included in the ISO recommendations. This is of great importance to the lumber-producing areas of Canada. I am citing these examples to indicate the importance of international standards to Canada as a trading nation.
One of the principal challenges lies in the field to international trade. The progressive reduction of tariffs in recent years, culminating in the Kennedy round which liberalized trade on some $40 billion worth of products, underscores the need for increased attention to international standards. While there are, of course, many barriers to the free flow of goods, few are more formidable than imcom-patible national standards.
When international standards exclude Canadian-made products, the loss of sales by Canadian manufacturers is a problem for the entire economy. For example, the standards for television sets in Europe are different from those in North America; they call for a different principle of scanning lines on 21774-40}
DEBATES	sols
Standards Council of Canada screens. Television sets described by these standards are not inherently better or worse than Canadian-made sets-they are just different. But the barrier to the sale of our television sets is as real as if the sets themselves had been excluded.
The way that we will promote more manufacturing industry in Canada is to achieve economy of scale by producing more goods that can be sold in greater quantities. Lack of international standards is an impairment of our ability to sell abroad and jeopardizes opportunities for Canadians to secure employment.
Standards and the benefits derived from them are so often taken for granted that their importance is frequently not appreciated until problems stemming from lack of standardization are encountered. The traveller abroad finds that an electrical appliance designed to operate on 100 volts at 60 cycles does not operate on 220 volts at 50 cycles. Members of parliamentary delegations know what a problem this presents. The purchaser of an imported article discovers that the metric sizes do not mesh with feet and inches.
Canada, whose position in the export market will depend increasingly upon its ability to market manufactured goods, cannot afford to ignore international collaboration in the setting of standards that can limit or enhance its trade prospects. In such participation there are fundamental guidelines, and the first basic is that international standards should not be formulated which for any reason through oversight or lack of initiative fail to take account of Canadian practices and thus limit sales potential where Canada has, or may have, a significant production or export capacity.
Second, the aim should be, where we are leading suppliers or where North American technology is pre-eminent, to have Canadian standards become the basis of the international standards, or to have them accepted as equal or superior to such standards. Third, where conflicts exist between North American and other standards, Canada should work for the establishment of a compromise international standard which can be incorporated into Canadian practices with a minimum of adjustment.
Finally, Canada should engage in international standards co-operation in certain areas of activity which may not be identifiable with the immediate Canadian interest. In particular, Canada should be prepared to assist in standards work of interest to developing


Standards Council of Canada countries. This is an area where we could really do great work, because we are in an unique position to work with these developing countries. They like us and we co-operate with them in so many other fields.
These countries, as they progressively establish national standards, are likely to accept those which have international acceptance. In the years ahead when development barriers have been overcome and new nations are able to finance much higher levels of imports, a selling country will be at a disadvantage if it has not participated in the standards established for the needs of those nations.
What we have here is a concern expressed by the government of Canada which is asking us to gird our loins against the international competitive battles that are to come, both internationally as well as on the domestic scene. To limit our standards setting to one organization with insufficient resources, commendable though that organization might be and despite the great work it has done in the past, I think would be limiting our vision with respect to the future of trade in the world.
Time does not permit me to discuss the importance of establishing standards in our own domestic industry; one of the speakers will, I am sure, be pleased to deal with this question. By way of concluding, Mr. Speaker, we have heard the argument advanced that in view of CSA's major reorganization and the expansion of its operation it is now capable of performing many functions assigned to the council. It is said, "We have been around for 50 years, but we suddenly had a great soulsearching and believe we can now do better". This is commendable, because within the framework of this organization this reappraisal of function can still continue and stand-ards-setting can proceed.
Yet it is a fair question to ask of those entering this claim: Why has this reorganization taken so long? Does it require the prospect of government action to inspire reorganization? What guarantee or assurance exists that the CSA or any other standards-setting organization in Canada, in two or three years time when a new set of executive members have come on the scene, will not alter its policy and gravitate once again to more limited goals? Surely it is impossible for the government to introduce a bill each time standards associations in Canada require a push, and then withdraw the proposal when the associations take some action. Surely what


Canada requires is a standards association that has a permanent base with firm, immediate and long-range objectives; a council which, in effect, will cast a wide umbrella over standards-writing in Canada. We need a representative council, an impartial council, a prestigious council.
The whole question of voluntary standards is of great importance to Canada. The extent to which we achieve a national posture in the field of standards will play a significant role in determining the level of economic activity in this country. Therefore, it is essential to have a national and impartial organization, not to write standards but to foster, promote and co-ordinate standardization activities and to bring together all interests with a view to providing an effective partnership between industry, consumer and government. This is the basic reason for establishing a standards council of Canada.
It is the view of many of us that the Canadian Standards Association has a major contribution to make to the work of the standards council-yes, and to other standards-writing organizations as well. This will enable the CSA and other organizations like it to play a larger and more effective role in formulating and promoting standards in Canada.
I urge the support of the members of the House for this bill. Let us get it to committee, produce as sound legislation as possible, and get on with the job.
