He took the Hazardous Products Act, but under that act things are not left to voluntary restraint; it sets out clearly and plainly substances that are dangerous to people and prohibits them. People move against this mandatory legislation at their peril because penalties for endangering the public are set out in the act.
We find the schizophrenic minister with another piece of legislation, which is part way through now, making that legislation mandatory because there is enough public pressure to make it mandatory but refusing to put another piece of legislation in because he wants it to be voluntary and that does not fit.
I suggest we are at a stage of development as an industrial nation where we cannot leave important standards on a voluntary basis. Consumers are demanding to know what they are getting in the way of sizes in children's clothing, the quality of fibres and standards for the different things they use around the home. We had car safety up for discussion yesterday. Consumers are getting to the point where they do not like things left to the good will, or lack of it, of manufacturers individually or collectively. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that voluntary standards mean unprotected consumers. Until we make the umbrella of standards cover everyone, we will have no adequate protection for the consumer.
As I say, I am still going to try to effect a divorce for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and get him in two pieces
Standards Council of Canada so that his right hand will not need to try and conceal what his left is doing, or vice versa. I want to see him protecting the consumers. The corporations do not need protection; they are able to look after themselves only too well. I want to know a lot more about why this legislation is being introduced. If the organization already existing has been doing a good job-and the minister waxed very lyrical about what a good job it had been doing-it has been on a voluntary basis. Now they come along with a government agency on a voluntary basis to supplant it.
The only reason I can think of for this measure is to make sure that standards will be left on a voluntary basis. This theme is running through the rest of the government's legislation. I refer to the water act. Over and over again I am reminded that there will not be, if this government follows its present intention, any national standards for clean water. Why not? Because manufacturers in one area want to keep the water so that they can, for a fee, continue dumping effluent into it.
The answer for the government is to get voluntary standards because mandatory ones would make it impossible for sectional interests to continue carrying on the way they are. That kind of philosophy leads the government into a rather unenviable position. It puts them in the position of "big brotherism", always watching very carefully the scene: they are always considering, measuring, white papering and task forcing. But what they are really doing is making very sure that the status quo will be maintained, and that the strong will be able to keep their position of entrenched strength with just enough restraint of a voluntary nature urged upon them so that the consumers can continue to breathe, even if the air is polluted and the water filthy to the point where they do not even like to wash their dishes in it.
Speaking from the standpoint of the consumer, I say we should get rid of this nonsense of believing that any favoured section of the community needs special protection today. The consumers are all of us, and until we make standards safe and uniform to cover us all, they will not be standards at all.
My colleagues have already dealt adequately and thoroughly with this matter, but after listening to the minister this morning-not the minister who is here but the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who is probably out dividing himself between consumers and corporations and not letting his

Canada Labour Code
right hand know what his left hand is doing- when he spoke about the Utopia that would be created under this bill, I was reminded of my childhood and a meeting of Labour Party supporters that took place in Winnipeg. One old fellow came to this meeting and painted pictures of Utopia and how everybody would be living in gingerbread houses, with water flowing from the mountains and 1,600 more kinds of birds than we have now twittering on all kinds of fruit trees, and the skies filled with signs and he would be rising up in his glory to contemplate the whole scene. I thought of that Utopia this morning when the minister was holding forth on the beauties of this legislation and its possibilities.
In this Garden of Eden that the minister portrayed there was one perfectly good serpent: that was the idea of voluntary standards, voluntary controls, voluntary restraints -all those voluntary things. Things are to be voluntary only for the big folk; the little ones are restrained by law. How much voluntary restraint have the little ones got in the matter of consumer credit, after last night's budget? Voluntary restraint is frozen injustice. This is what I am afraid of as a result of this legislation.

He said: Mr. Speaker, we may have come out of the Garden of Eden but there are still a few serpents around that we should do our best to slay. Indeed, we now have before us a bill that relates to another set of standards.
I should like to remind the House that during this session we have broken with tradition a bit in that three of four or maybe
[Mrs. Maclnnis.l
even five or six private members' bills and resolutions have received concurrence during the private members' hour. In some cases that has meant simply the referral of a bill to an appropriate committee so that it could be studied further. I hope that this new tradition might continue this afternoon. Accordingly, with that fervent hope I shall present this bill in the most reasonable way I can. That is easy to do because it seeks to enact into legislation a principle with which we all agree.
e (4:00 p.m.)
The proposal of Bill C-43 is that the Canada Labour (Standards) Code be amended. That code is the legislation which lays down standards regarding minimum wages, hours of work, general holidays, vacations with pay and so on. But there are a few gaps in that legislation and this bill seeks to fill one of those gaps.
This bill proposes that within the area of employment that comes under federal labour jurisdiction there be a requirement that any employer who wishes to discharge or lay off an employee, provided the employee has been with that employer for three months or more, Shall give two weeks' notice to the employee. The employee, of course, can be given two weeks' full pay in lieu of that notice, but the bill spells out that nothing less than that shall be given to such employee.
I point out immediately that the bill has in it a clause which shows how to work out full pay for two weeks. It also makes it clear that if the person who has received notice were to work overtime during that two weeks, he would be entitled to more than the two weeks normal pay. It also has in it a very important provision saying that nothing in this bill shall affect any greater rights set out in a collective agreement. One or two other points are covered in the bill, but in the main I have indicated what it seeks to do. It seeks to establish as a principle in federal labour legislation that provided an employee has been for three months with the same employer, that employee shall not be summarily discharged but shall be given at least two weeks' notice or two weeks' full pay in lieu of that notice.
When I stand here and present this bill to the House I do not feel like shouting from the house tops that it is the most wonderful bill I have ever drafted. As a matter of fact, I think it asks for far too little. I think for a person to be given only two weeks' notice or two


weeks' pay before being turned out into the cold of unemployment is really not enough, and I would not be at all unhappy if hon. members of other parties or members of my own party were to say that the bill should be amended to provide for three or four weeks' pay in such cases. But I have learned around here that you have to ask for a minimum in order to get something started. I hope the House generally will see this bill as introducing a principle that ought to be written into our federal labour legislation.
Every time a bill dealing with either of the labour codes comes before us-and it might deal with the standards code or the safety code-we have to make it clear that the federal labour law does not affect all the working people of Canada; it affects only those who come under federal labour jurisdiction as set out in the British North America Act. The main groups, of course, are those who work on our railways, on steamships, in banking, communications and a few occupations like that. The list is rather long, but even when you take all those covered by the list you find that you are speaking about only 10 per cent of the working force of Canada. The other 90 per cent of our workers are covered under provincial labour laws.
Nevertheless, it has been a fact of history in Canada that the federal government is able to give a lead, and what we write into federal labour law not only protects those who come under it but sets the pattern which in due course one province after another finds it expedient to follow. In this way, over the years, we have managed to build up a labour law which is not too much at variance as among the various provinces or between the provinces and the federal government. I should say that it is not always the federal government that gives the lead. In some instances provinces may give the lead, and I suppose this is good in a federal state like ours. It is good that patterns are set both ways.
We have been made aware in recent days of a number of instances of plants closing down and of sections of the labour force losing their jobs immediately. I will not quarrel at this moment with the answer the government makes when it says that some of these matters we have complained about come under provincial jurisdiction. The point I am trying to make is that even though many of these instances fall under provincial jurisdiction, surely it is a good idea to provide that under federal labour law workers
Canada Labour Code
cannot be discharged with almost no notice and without any pay for any period of time.
It is also a fact that most of the employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction, particularly railway workers, airline workers and groups like that, are rather well organized. They have this kind of protection. But there are still many who are under federal labour jurisdiction who do not have this protection. Because we do not have the principle enunciated in this bill written into laws which govern at the federal level, I submit there is a significant gap in the labour laws of this country.
As I say, I cannot imagine any member of this House not agreeing with the principle of the bill. I can imagine some questions about its details. The most significant criticism would be one that people like me would levy-that it does not go far enough. But surely in principle it is good. It is good that we in Parliament should say that so far as we can enact by legislation, nobody shall lose his job without being given either two weeks notice or two weeks pay in lieu thereof. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope the House, after discussing the bill during this hour, will decide it is a good idea to give it second reading so that it can be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration for further study.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know what Garden of Eden the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was referring to in his opening remarks. However, I commend the hon. member for bringing to the attention of the House, through the medium of this bill, a situation which merits the attention of every hon. member. His proposal is in the form of an amendment to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and if adopted it would mean that employees would be compensated in cases of discharge or lay-off and employers would be forced to give employees due notice when their services were no longer required because of the closing of business, industry or for any other cause.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I do not hesitate to agree with the need for legislation to bring about a uniform policy governing every employer of labour in every part of Canada. I agree with the hon. member that the principle of this bill is good, the purpose of which, as I have already said, is to provide compensation for workers losing their jobs through no fault of their own. In this age


Canada Labour Code
of automation it oftens happens that a particular job is eliminated by machinery or by the closing of an industry, or it can cause loss of seniority or other rights and privileges due to employees by virtue of length of service.
A few years ago I supported in this House a similar measure for the benefit of railwaymen who had lost their jobs as a result of changes brought about by the abandonment of branch lines or automation. The purpose was to have the railways pay the railwaymen being rehabilitated with new skills, the expense of moving to a new job, pension compensation for early retirement-if that was considered the better plan-or such other compensation deemed best for the re-establishment of discharged employees.
Public benefits through unemployment insurance to qualified workers seeking employment were also intended to help the displaced worker through the period in which he might be unemployed. In recent years, through collective bargaining, the concept of severance pay and the availability of unemployment insurance have been merged in a variety of ways. Workers who are laid off with or without the expectation that the layoff will be permanent are also realizing, in cash or in vested rights and fringe benefits, what they stand to lose, together with compensation for wages lost. Traditional severance pay plans provide a money payment in a lump sum or instalments to workers whose employment has been terminated.
I recall that during the period when I was mayor of the city of Fort William our city-owned telephone service was changed over from manual to the present dial system. At that time we had approximately 70 telephone operators on the payroll, and with the installation of the dial system some 60 operators lost their jobs. The city council decided to give each of them severance remuneration, the amount of which was settled according to the months and years of employment of each individual. With a complete severance of the employment relationship, as in the case of the Fort William telephone girls, payments are such that only permanent separation is applicable. These awards are variously referred to as severance pay, termination pay, dismissal allowance, separation benefit, and lay-off allowance where lay-off implies permanent lay-off. Under such plans the payment of benefits is not contingent on the worker remaining unemployed.
The primary purpose of supplemental unemployment benefit plans is to provide

weekly allowances to workers on lay-offs to supplement unemployment compensation. Usually the lay-off is not considered permanent, that is, both employer and worker expect the worker to be recalled on the job. Unlike traditional severance pay plans, supplemental unemployment benefits are paid only if the worker is unemployed.
The publication "Labour Standards in Canada" of December, 1967, reports that four provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and Quebec, have legislation requiring an employer to give notice of termination of employment. The legislation is contained in part 3 of the Employment Standards Act of Manitoba, in the Minimum Wage Acts of Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia and in the Civil Code of Quebec.
As the hon. member who introduced this bill knows, in Manitoba an employer or employee in any work or occupation except farming must give notice of termination of employment, and unless a person is paid less frequently than once a month the period of notice required is one regular paid period. If employees are paid less often than once a month, reasonable notice must be given. But notice of termination is not required if an employee is hired for a fixed period.
In Saskatchewan an employer is forbidden to discharge, unless for just cause other than shortage of work, or lay off an employee for three months or more without giving him at least one week's written notice. An employee who has been given written notice is entitled, in respect of the period of notice, to his actual earnings in a week.
In Nova Scotia, as in Saskatchewan, an employer is required to give an employee with three months' continuous service or more, at least one week's written notice of termination of employment or lay-off. The provisions in these two provinces are the same so far as the employer's obligation is concerned. The Nova Scotia act also requires an employee with three months' service or more to give his employer at least one week's notice of his intention to terminate his employment.
In Quebec the Civil Code requires a domestic servant, journeyman or labourer engaged by the week, month or year to give one week's notice of termination of employment if hired by the week, two weeks' notice if hired by the month, and a month's notice if hired by the year. The employer must give similar notice where an employee's services are no


longer required. In lieu of notice the employer may pay the employee the wages he would have earned during the notice period.
At the forty-seventh session of the International Labour Organization held at Geneva on June 26, 1963, certain recommendations were made concerning termination of employment. Some of these recommendations are as follows:
Termination of employment should not take place unless there is a valid reason for such termination connected with the capacity or conduct of the worker or based on the operational requirements of the undertaking, establishment or service.
A worker who feels that his employment has been unjustifiably terminated should be entitled unless the matter has been satisfactorily determined through such procedures within the undertaking, establishment or service, as may exist or be established consistent with this recommendation, to appeal, within a reasonable time, against that termination with the assistance, where the worker so requests, of a person representing him to a body established under a collective agreement or to a neutral body such as a court, an arbitrator, an arbitration committee or a similar body.
Subparagraph (1) should not be construed as implying that the neutral body should be empowered to intervene in the determination of the size of the work force of the undertaking, establishment or service.
A worker whose employment is to be terminated should be entitled to a reasonable period of notice or compensation in lieu thereof.
Some form of income protection should be provided for workers whose employment has been terminated; such protection may include unemployment insurance or other forms of social security, or severance allowance or other types of separation benefits paid for by the employer, or a combination of benefits depending upon national laws or regulations, collective agreements and the personnel policy of the employer.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
These recommendations concerning termination of employment are from the General Conference of the International Labour Organization in Geneva. As to the recommendation about methods of implementation, it was agreed it might be made through national laws, regulations, collective agreements, work rules arbitration awards, court decisions or in such other manner consistent with national practice as might be appropriate under national conditions.
Should the whole burden in these cases fall on the employer? That is a question which might well be taken up by a parliamentary committee for study and recommendation. Industries such as the Dunlop plant in Toronto, where it was recently reported that layoffs would occur, have certain obligations to
Canada Labour Code
their employees; such obligations are bound to arise whenever the position of employees is affected by the installation of labour-saving installations.
According to a news item in today's issue of the Globe and Mail, Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company of Canada Limited, Toronto, is to shut down along with plants at Val-leyfield and Saint Hyacinthe in the province of Quebec. Announcements of this kind are bound to raise questions of considerable importance in this era of industrial change. Workers in the transportation industry, no less than workers in factories, are affected by them.
The threatened run-through by Canadian National at Nakeena in northwestern Ontario is an example. If carried out, it would impose real hardship on families living in this community. It would be a case of sacrificing the welfare of a small community on the cross of efficiency. I express the hope that it will not be necessary for the railways to take this drastic step.
Down through the years delegation after delegation has appeared before ministers and heads of departments to protest the curtailment of railway services, including express and telegraph service, and to discuss other matters of great concern to the men and women employed in our once great railway system. Sometimes their pleas have been directed to situations in other industries; I have in mind the occasion when the Canada Car plant in my constituency was about to close down due to lack of orders. Invariably these delegations were well received and a sympathetic hearing was given to their anguished pleas that consideration should be extended to workers on the verge of being displaced.
The bill before us today will not put an end to the displacement of workers because of shutdowns, automation or other causes, but at least it will offer some assistance at a time when help is most needed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in the debate on the motion for second reading and referral to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration of Bill C-43 which would incorporate into the Canada Labour Code a regulation compelling the employer to pay two weeks' salary to a laid-off employee.
I should like to tell the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that I sup-


Canada Labour Code
port the principle of his bill. I am glad to see him taking part in the debate. In a democratic system, it is normal that a man who is laid off due to an improvement aimed at greater efficiency, to cost shaving or to automation receive a payment.
I have a few things to say about labour relations in our country. There are two aspects to the question which should not be mistaken.
Labour groups, formed to protect the rights of workers, sometimes negotiate agreements with employers in the name of employees. But there is another category of workers in Canada who do not belong to unions and who represent 55 or 60 per cent of the Canadian labour force, although those figures may not be exact.
The rights of unionized workers are protected to some extent. The law recognizes their right to strike. It establishes a certain procedure for the approval of collective agreements when the two parties are at odds. The worker who belongs to an union can also make sure that the latter has made some investigations concerning his type of work, in order that the industry where he is working will not simply become obsolete and go out of business.
I will now discuss a quite important aspect. It is perhaps the most important in most cases. It often happens that on account of the attitude of the employer or the union, we are led to believe that money or wages is the most important consideration.
All those who bargain with employees know very well that the financial aspects of a collective agreement, at a given time, have less importance. Labour conditions would come first. Among them are many small practical considerations. I mean hours of work and retraining.
I am also referring to the problems of human relations that can arise between the foreman and the men and the way to settle them. Collective agreements specify recognized means to settle grievances or other similar difficulties.
There are also the provisions concerning leisure. In Canada, apparently, we are not yet smart enough to realize that we need more spare time, and this at all levels of our society, including workers, members of Parliament, executives, etc.
Canadians do not seem to have yet recognized the importance of leisure time. In fact, it is most important not to work 60 or 70

hours per week and to devote one hour or-two per day to recreation. This time can be devoted to reading, or to any other physical activity. One can also devote his spare time to an intellectual activity.	.
In negotiating new collective agreements this particular aspect is beginning to be considered. Indeed, it is believed that the worker must stop work two hours a day in order to relax his mind or devote himself to physical exercise. Therefore, he is in top shape and works twice as fast and much more carefully. He feels more at ease. Furthermore, this is very good for his health. In Canada, some unions are concerned about that.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I am mainly concerned about those workers who do not benefit from the provisions of collective agreements. Some of those people are even to be found in the employ of large companies, in forestry for example, where employees are not members of any union. Sometimes, when three lumberjacks use the same power-saw, the foreman says: I can no longer keep more than one worker. So, the other two must leave. They must then give up their job, because they do not have the $200 that are necessary for the purchase of a power-saw.
What is more serious, is that the employer tells the Unemployment Insurance Commission that the worker has given up his job voluntarily. That is obviously an extreme case, but it may happen. In fact, in my district especially, if often happens that unfair advantage is taken of some people by large companies. The principle of the bill submitted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre appears to be wise, because the object of the proposal is to prevent exploitation of the worker.
Also, a good many workers are not in the employ of large companies and it could be argued that they allow inefficient undertakings to carry on their activities. Such businesses should not exist since the employers do not do enough for their employees and do not make available to them a useful apprenticeship. In short, the employee is the loser because after 10 or 15 years, the business goes bankrupt. The owner always succeeds in coming off without too much harm but it is always the employee who pays the piper.
I agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just said, as what, he is proposing only amounts to an absolute minimum. As I said, I approve the principle


of the bill before us. Provincial governments should also adopt similar legislation and all employers should be completed to include such provisions in collective agreements. If an employee works for a company or an individual for five or six years, the employer should be concerned about his security and give him severance pay when he is laid off to enable him to support himself for three weeks or a month-

-the hon. member says he should be able to support himself for two weeks. I feel it would be justified to extend this period to three weeks or a month in some cases.
I am pleased that this bill is now under consideration. I support the motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It is not often that I can support him, although I always hold his opinions in high respect. However, we do not share the same political views. In any case, I am glad to back him up. I know he is striving to improve the workers' lot, to get them better protection by society. The challenge our society will be facing in the 70's and even in the 80's will be to enact legislation that will better serve the workers' interests. Besides, that problem should urgently be solved.
The hon. member knows that things will not necessarily change through legislation. Canadians, and more particularly the employers, must recognize the principle to the effect that employees are not machines to be be paid $40 or $100 per week. They must no longer be told to go when the work is done.
I think that in the years to come, the challenge for our society, in Canada as well as in the United States, will be to find, by means of legislation or otherwise, how to protect the interests of unorganized workers.
When we speak of collective agreements, a lot of people think that it is a threat to economy, but I do not agree. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) said recently that strikes were the price to pay for democracy. It may be an over-simple manner to visualize things but the philosophy under this approach is not for all that devoid of any sense. Many civil servants are against the right to strike, but under a democratic system, it must be recognized that the worker has to protect his interests, his rights and his privileges, which is getting more and more urgent.
Today, we are in an era of automation and I could quote as an example the case of a
Canada Labour Code
company that would settle in a small town that I know, but because its technology is not developed, could ruin the life of all those people not only financially but socially as well. This phenomenon exists in certain parts of Canada. In my riding there are some small towns that a single company could turn into ghost towns.
However, when employees become well organized and see to it that the company that hires them is going into research in order to progress through automation, that company will not be able to state one fine day that it can no longer operate.
I therefore say again to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that I agree with the principle of the bill. I trust that some time in the future the provinces will adopt a similar bill, that it might no longer be necessary to adopt laws such as this one, because what I have just dealt with will have become a working condition recognized throughout the country by all employers.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE PROVISION FOR NOTICE AND PAYMENT TO EMPLOYEES WHEN LAID OFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for introducing this bill. I know that in so doing he has drawn attention to a situation in Canada which must leave many of us very unhappy. Probably most of us thought that this matter was already taken care of by various regulations, or perhaps even just by custom throughout the country; but obviously it is not properly taken care of.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) has pointed out that only four provinces in Canada have regulations in the provincial jurisdiction covering this question. In other provinces of Canada and elsewhere it seems to be the custom that an employee is given notice according to the length of his normal pay period; that is to say, if he is employed by the week, it is assumed that he is entitled to a week's notice. If he is paid on the basis of every two weeks, twice a month, or monthly, he is entitled to notice for the length of his pay period.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We must all recognize that this indefinite situation leaves a great deal to be desired, and it leaves both the employer and the employee wondering what is the fact today. In many instances it must leave the employee the victim of an unscrupulous employer who takes advantage of a situation, which may not


Canada Labour Code
be written into law, to dismiss an employee without the kind of notice to which he is entitled. I think we have come a long way from the kind of situation in the past when employees were treated as chattels and could be dismissed on a moment's notice or at the whim of an employer. We now treat employees with some deference and respect for the responsibilities they have. I commend the bill the hon. member has introduced today.
I understand that the Department of Labor is now considering legislation, or a regulation of this kind. I think it is important, now that the bill has been introduced, that we look at the inferences in it and consider what is being done in other jurisdictions, in order that these thoughts may be of use to us in developing similar legislation and regulations in Canada. I believe there are some things in the bill that need improving. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre himself said, there are in the bill some things that could be improved. I notice the absence of enforcement regulations in the bill-enforcement on the part of the employer and the employee.

I
appreciate that clarification. The hon. member has much more experience in these things and has been in this House many more years than I have. I appreciate his clarification on that point because I have experienced situations of this kind. Sometimes the fault is not that of the employer: quite often the fault is the employee's because he decides suddenly to leave the employer. The hon. member mentions this matter in section 34H. I am glad to see it is there, because the situation I have mentioned could work a hardship.
Lack of responsibility sometimes by employees could be a distinct detriment to a business that needs the services of a skilled employee and suddenly finds it does not have that service available. Responsibility has to be shown by the employee as well as the employer. I appreciate that this provision is in

the bill, and I hope that when this idea is propelled further, regulations will be put into effect which will make this measure enforceable.
I was very surprised to discover that there are only form provinces in Canada which have regulations of this kind. As the hon. member for Fort William pointed out, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and Quebec have such regulations. The regulations for giving notice do not apply if a general custom or practice which is contrary to the terms of the act prevails in an industry. These are some of the provisions that exist when different conditions as to notice are established by collective agreement. If employment is terminated during an employee's first two weeks on a job, notice is not required unless the employer and the employee have agreed in writing that the requirements of the act shall apply. An employer is permitted to establish a practice whereby employment may be terminated with a shorter period of notice than that provided for in the act or in provincial acts, and the practice is considered to have been established one month after he has posted notice of these things.
It seems to me that regulations of this kind leave a great many loopholes that need to be filled. These matters have to be spelled out in a better way. It is true that complaints can be placed before provincial ministers, say within a 90-day period, and procedures are laid down under some provincial regulations for so doing. In Saskatchewan an employer is forbidden to discharge, unless for just cause other than a shortage of work, or lay off an employee who has been in his service continuously for three months or more, without giving him at least one week's written notice. A lay-off is defined as a temporary dispensation of an employee's service for a period of more than six consecutive days.
In Nova Scotia, as in Saskatchewan, an employer is required to give an employee with three months' continuous service or more at least one week's notice of termination of employment or lay-off. The provisions in these two provinces are similar so far as employee's obligations are concerned. The Nova Scotia act requires an employee with three months' service or more to give his employer at least one week's notice of his intention to terminate his employment. Those are some of the provincial regulations we must consider, together with international thinking on this subject. We gain much of our information about labour relations and much


of our direction,, initiative and inspiration from the International Labour Organization. They have studied this matter and have come up with recommendations, specifically as a result of a meeting that was held in 1963. I should like to discuss some of these points because I think they are valuable and can be of guidance to us in considering this matter.
It is suggested in the International Labour Organization agreement that the effect of their recommendations can be brought in through national laws, collective agreements, regulations, work rules, arbitration awards, court decisions or in such other manner consistent with national practice as may be appropriate under national conditions. I shall refer to some of the things they feel we in Canada and those in other parts of the world should be doing. Let me refer to the question of a reasonable period of notice. Section 7 of the agreement says:
A worker whose employment is to be terminated should be entitled to a reasonable period of notice or compensation in lieu thereof.
During the period of notice the worker should, as far as practicable, be entitled to a reasonable amount of time off without loss in pay in order to seek other employment.
Such a provision might well be included in a bill of this kind. If an employee knows he will have to find other employment, it seems fair that he should be allowed a reasonable period in which to seek a new position. He should have the opportunity to go for an interview or fill in an application for employment. The next paragraph of section 7 states:
The worker whose employment has been terminated should be entitled to receive, on request, at the time of the termination, a certificate from the employer specifying the dates of his engagement and the termination and the type or types of work on which he was employed.
This is another very useful provision. It suggests that nothing unfavourable to the worker should be inserted in the certificate. There is in the suggested regulations a point about an employee's misconduct. I think this point should be looked at because it does bear on the question.
In case of dismissal or serious misconduct, a period of notice or compensation in lieu thereof need not be required, and the severence allowance or other types of separation benefits paid for by the employer, where applicable, may be withheld.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It makes suggestions regarding misconduct because these are questions employers will ask, and I think they are entitled to ask them because the government must act on this
Canada Labour Code
matter for both labour and management. I think we stand between the two. The agreement reads in part:
Dismissal for serious misconduct should take place only in cases where the employer cannot in good faith be expected to take any other course.
An employer should be deemed to have waived his right to dismiss for serious misconduct if such action has not been taken within a reasonable time after he has become aware of serious misconduct.
A worker should be deemed to have waived his right to appeal against dismissal for serious misconduct if he has not appealed within a reasonable time after he has been notified of the dismissal.
Before a decision to dismiss a worker for serious misconduct becomes finally effective, the worker should be given an opportunity to state his case promptly, with the assistance where appropriate of a person representing him.
Those are all very valuable recommendations which should be included in a properly drafted bill when the time comes. Some exceptions are noted in the ILO recommendations. I think they are of interest to us today. They are:
workers engaged for a specified period of time or a specified task in cases in which, owing to the nature of the work to be effected, the employment relationship cannot be of indeterminate duration.
We could all readily cite examples where that might be the situation. Certainly, if a man is hired for snow removal-perhaps not in Ottawa but in some other parts of the country-his work is of a temporary nature and perhaps is not entitled to such consideration. I see that the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) takes exception to my comments about the weather in Ottawa. Another member from the Vancouver area suggests that in Vancouver the man would be completely unemployed. The following are the other exceptions:
workers serving a period of probation determined in advance and of reasonable duration;
You can hire a man for a specified period which might be more than three months but which would be a specific period of time. The next exception is as follows: workers engaged on a casual basis for a short period; and
public servants engaged in the administration of the State to the extent only that constitutional provisions preclude the application to them of one or more provisions of this recommendation.
Those are some of the very excellent recommendations put out by the International Labour Organization in 1963. I think they are


Canada Labour Code
worth a great deal of attention by the government when a bill of this kind is drawn up by the committee.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE PROVISION FOR NOTICE AND PAYMENT TO EMPLOYEES WHEN LAID OFF
speechtext: I hope it will. As I mentioned earlier, I understand the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) is considering regulations of this kind, so whether or not this bill goes forward I am sure the matter will receive favourable consideration. We can all be glad this is the case, because I am sure there is agreement on all sides of the House that legislation of this kind should become part of the legal structure in Canada. It is a shock to us to find that only four provinces have similar provisions in their legislation and that the federal government does not have them in its federal labour code. This bill is long overdue, and I heartily support it. I hope it goes forward, and I commend the hon. member for having introduced it.
